Subject: Dedicated commit throughput & latency — clarification and next steps

Hi Sean / team,

Thanks again for the walkthrough yesterday — Sophie here from Acme Health. We liked the direction on Dedicated pools. Before we loop procurement, we need clarity on three items so that my engineering and procurement teams can sign off:

1) Throughput guarantees — are these expressed as tokens/sec or requests/sec? How do you size GPU pools vs. a mixed workload (short chat queries + long generation jobs)?
2) Latency targets — what latency distributions do you guarantee (p50/p95/p99) and how are they measured?
3) Measurement methodology — during acceptance testing and ongoing billing, what tests are run, how long are sampling windows, and how do you account for cache warm-up / KV cache effects?

Also, attached is our initial traffic profile and a draft commit size. We'd like a banded commit (reserved tokens/day) with a pricing discount schedule tied to commit size. Can you include a worked example for 12-month and 36-month commits including any ramp periods?

Attachment: acme_proposed_commit_v1.xlsx (spreadsheet, 92 KB)

Can we aim to have an agreed test plan by end of next week? Procurement will need the precise acceptance criteria to approve the PO.

Thanks,

Thanks Sophie — great questions. High level answers below; Rishi/Camila/Laura, please add details / commercial language.

Summary (short):
- We define guarantees at the token/sec level for committed GPU pools and at request/sec for API route-based SLAs. Tokens/sec maps directly to GPU provisioning for mixed workloads.
- Latency targets are contractual for p95 on a per-route basis; we publish p50/p95/p99 in Console for transparency. For Dedicated commits we can guarantee p95 <= X ms for a target token rate — specifics depend on model family and sequence length assumptions.
- Measurement: acceptance runs use a combined synthetic + sampled-production approach: synthetic load with representative input distributions + 1–2 days of production sampling to capture cache effects. We run a 30-minute acceptance window per test vector after a warming phase.

Sizing & example:
- If your profile (attached) is 60% short chat (~20–60 tokens), 30% medium (~200 tokens), 10% long (~800 tokens), a ruled-of-thumb mapping is ~1x V100-equivalent GPU per X tokens/sec — we'll compute exact GPU counts after we agree on model variant and quantization.
- For a 12-month commit we typically offer a 12–18% discount on top of hosted list, with deeper discounts for 24/36-month commitments. Discounts are tiered by committed tokens/day.

Acceptance test components (we attach a proposed plan):
- Controlled synthetic run (tooling: rdw-load-sim) to validate sustained tokens/sec for 30 minutes, with periodic KV-cache invalidation to measure steady-state throughput.
- Sampled production playback (sanitized) for 24 hours to validate latency distribution under realistic arrival patterns.
- Ops & engineering signoff criteria: pass synthetic window at >= 95% of committed tokens/sec and p95 latency target within agreed band.

I'll attach a short test plan next. If this looks reasonable, Laura can draft the commercial language for the SOW and Rishi can propose SLA credit mechanics.

Adding the SLA and measurement detail. Sophie — I'll keep the language procurement-friendly.

How we measure (short):
- Units: primary guarantee expressed as sustained tokens/sec for the committed GPU pool over a rolling 1-hour window; secondary, per-route req/sec SLOs for critical endpoints.
- Sampling & warm-up: we treat the first 10 minutes of any acceptance window as warm-up and exclude it from the statistics. For production monitoring we compute rolling 1h and 24h windows and report the worst-case 95th percentile for the billing period.
- Test harness: we use our internal rdw-benchmark tool (open to an audited run) that simulates weighted traffic mixes. For acceptance we run: warm-up (10m) -> sustained load (30m) -> soak (20m). Failure is >5% drop vs committed tokens/sec or p95 latency > target for the sustained window.
- Cache considerations: we explicitly run with cold start and warm-KV cache phases; the acceptance pass must meet two criteria: (a) cold-start baseline not exceeding an agreed multiplier of the target latency, and (b) warm-state sustained throughput matching the committed tokens/sec.

Credit calculation & remediation:
- If we miss the committed throughput in a billing window, credits apply proportional to the shortfall. Example: 5% shortfall -> 5% of that billing period's committed token charge credited. Extreme cases trigger joint remediation & capacity uplift.

I'll draft proposed SLA language for the SOW and attach a sample clause. Laura — can you confirm commercial language for ramp and termination?

Sophie — operationalizing the acceptance run and ongoing measurement is my wheelhouse. A few practical notes and the exact steps we'll run during the acceptance window: 

Operational runbook (acceptance):
- Preflight: sync on model hash, quantization profile, and exact routes (we need your team to agree which endpoints count toward the commit).
- Environment: isolated Dedicated pool with telemetry hooks to Console (token counters, per-route latency histograms, and KV cache hit-rate).
- Test steps:
  1) Sanity checks (10m): verify model loads, KV cache empty.
  2) Cold-start pass (10m): run small burst to capture baseline latencies.
  3) Sustained throughput pass (30m): targeted tokens/sec per agreed mix; we collect p50/p95/p99 and token counters.
  4) Warm-state verification (20m): after KV priming, re-run sustained pass.
- Acceptance criteria: sustained pass must hit >=95% of target tokens/sec and p95 latency must be within +/- 20% of the contractual p95 target for the warm-state pass.

What counts as outage vs. capacity variance:
- Outage: >5 consecutive minutes where the pool is unable to serve at all or control-plane eviction happens.
- Capacity variance: sustained degradation below threshold but service still reachable (handled via credits).

Scheduling & timeline:
- We recommend a one-week window for scheduling (to coordinate on-site/remote test runs). We can do weekday runs or a weekend window to avoid noisy production traffic.

Links & artifacts: will upload the runbook and scripts to a shared Drive after you confirm the models/routes. Example link: https://drive.redwood.ai/share/ACM-138/runbook (will provide access once you confirm).
